newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Poll offers Algeria chance to adjust bloody path.
newsitem.headline: Poll offers Algeria chance to adjust bloody path.

text.p: The entry into Algeria's parliament of Islamists and secularists outside the mould of traditional republicans gives Algeria's leaders a chance to start forging consensus after years of strife, diplomats and analysts said.

They do not expect the rainbow make-up of the new National Assembly that emerged from last Thursday's general election to end the more than five years of violence in which about 60,000 people have died.
But, they said, it could lay the ground for further isolating the Moslem rebels and ending the sometimes ambiguous stand of some political parties towards them.

The poll, although dominated by the pro-government National Democratic Rally (RND), saw 103 Moslem fundamentalists, 38 secularists, 11 independents and four leftwingers enter parliament for the first time in this nation of 29 million Moslems.
"Whatever the complaints over the poll results, Moslem fundamentalism was the great winner in the legislative elections," said Hassane Zerouky, editor of the secular-leaning Le Matin newspaper.
He said fundamentalists would use parliament to boost their political fortunes at a time of disillusionment over President Liamine Zeroual's promises to bring about quick change.
Diplomats said the radical Islamist score was the surprise of the election, reflected in the legal, religious-oriented Nadha party's 34 seats in the parliament.
"Nahda is hard-core militant Islam. The party seems to have succeeded in winning back militants from the FIS (Islamic Salvation Front)," a western diplomat said.
The FIS, which took a huge lead in Algeria's last general election in 1991 before it was cancelled by the military-backed authorities, is outlawed and could not contest this ballot.

"This election sanctioned a strong Islamist current in Algeria and mirrored the existence of other political currents able to coexist and compete without resorting to violence," said a leading Algerian analyst who asked not to be named.
The use of Islam as a party platform to attract voters -- used before with such success by the FIS -- was barred under laws enacted before this election.
But the clearly Islam-oriented Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS), formerly called Hamas, of Mahfoud Nahnah emerged as the second biggest party with 69 seats, after the RND's 155.

In what to many observers was another surprise, the former ruling National Liberation Front (FLN), consigned by many to the dustbin of history, won 64 seats to emerge as the fourth largest party in the 380 seat assembly.

An official with a western tank-think group, who travelled in Algiers to watch the election, said the FLN score showed the beginning of rejuvenation, bringing new generations of activists receptive of modern democracy and disgruntled by the party old guard.
A senior Western diplomat said opposition party leaders, who bitterly laid into each other before the poll, would now have to learn to operate through consensus on the main issues.
"The opposition has to do its part to coexist," he said.

But analysts are still guessing about Zeroual's next moves for a working understanding between a weak parliament, executive government and political parties, to spark hope among Algerians who mainly voted for peace and accountable government.
Under the constitution the president has a free hand to name a head of government. It is unclear if the prime minister should be from the biggest party in the parliament.
"The next prime minister and his cabinet will tell about Zeroual's intentions, about whether he wants to break the status quo and widen the government base," one diplomat said.
One analyst said the worst case scenario would be a coalition government between the RND of Zeroual supporters and the former ruling FLN.
"Most Algerians...will read that as proof that the regime has decided to block efforts to forge an alternative to the status quo," he said.
They would believe authorities wanted an election purely "to win support from the main Western powers more interested in political stability than a developed democracy."
